Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\gamma>0$, let
$C=-\Delta-\gamma/|\cdot|$ on $H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ be as above, let
$(\psi_{nlm})$ be the bound eigenfunctions of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-negative-subspace-completeness-and-degeneracy]], and for
$i=1,2,3$ define the coordinate multiplication operator
$$Q_i\psi:=(\xi\mapsto\xi_i\,\psi(\xi)),\qquad D(Q_i):=\{\psi\in L^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C):\xi_i\psi\in L^2\}.$$
Write also $Q_0:=x_3$ and $Q_\pm:=(x_1\pm ix_2)/\sqrt2$. Then:

(a) each $Q_i$ is self-adjoint on $D(Q_i)$, the domain is a proper dense subspace of $L^2$, and every bound state satisfies $\psi_{nlm}\in D(Q_i)$, with $\|Q_i\psi_{nlm}\|_2^2=\int_0^\infty r^2|u_{nl}(r)|^2dr\cdot\int_{S^2}|\Omega_iY_{lm}(\Omega)|^2d\sigma(\Omega)<\infty$;

(b) for all labels and each $q\in\{-1,0,1\}$ the matrix element $\langle\psi_{n'l'm'},Q_q\psi_{nlm}\rangle$ is absolutely convergent and factors as
$$\langle\psi_{n'l'm'},Q_q\psi_{nlm}\rangle=\Bigl(\int_0^\infty r\,u_{n'l'}(r)\overline{u_{nl}(r)}\,dr\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_{S^2}Y_{l'm'}(\Omega)\overline{Q_q(\Omega)\,Y_{lm}(\Omega)}\,d\sigma(\Omega)\Bigr),$$
where $Q_q(\Omega)$ denotes the restriction of the polynomial $Q_q$ to $S^2$;

(c) the angular factor vanishes unless $l'=l+1,\ m'=m+q$ or $l\ge1,\ l'=l-1,\ m'=m+q$; these are necessary conditions only: no assertion is made that an allowed pair has nonzero radial integral, and no transition probability is asserted or computed;

(d) for the oscillator: with $\omega>0$, $\ell:=\sqrt{\hbar/(m\omega)}$, the complete orthonormal family $(\psi_n^{\mathrm{osc}})$ of [[thm-nrqm-oscillator-oscillator-scaling-and-exact-realization]] and the position operator $X$ (multiplication by $\ell y$ in the scaled variable) one has
$$X\psi_n^{\mathrm{osc}}=\frac{\ell}{\sqrt2}\bigl(\sqrt n\,\psi_{n-1}^{\mathrm{osc}}+\sqrt{n+1}\,\psi_{n+1}^{\mathrm{osc}}\bigr),$$
so $\langle\psi_{n'}^{\mathrm{osc}},X\psi_n^{\mathrm{osc}}\rangle$ vanishes unless $n'=n\pm1$, with the displayed coefficients; in particular the oscillator position matrix elements are supported on a single step $|\Delta n|=1$, while the Coulomb selection rules constrain only $\Delta l$ and $\Delta m$ and leave the radial integral free.

This item concerns matrix elements of multiplication operators on $L^2$ and
their finiteness and selection rules; it asserts no absorption, emission or
transition rate and no physical interpretation.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space.

- For $0<p<\infty$, define an equivalence relation on $\mathcal L^p(\mu)$ by
  $$f\sim g\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad f-g\in\mathcal N(\mu),$$
  and write $L^p(\mu)$ for the set of classes $[f]$.
- For $p=\infty$, define the same relation on $L^\infty(\mu)$ and again write
  $L^\infty(\mu)$ for the set of classes.

Thus an element of $L^p(\mu)$ is an almost-everywhere equivalence class of
measurable representatives.

When $1\le p\le\infty$, the displayed set quotient agrees with the usual
quotient-vector-space construction of
[[def-quotient-vector-space-and-canonical-projection]].

For $0<p<1$, the same class notation is used; under its stated choice hypothesis, the later item
[[thm-the-l-p-distance-for-zero-less-p-less-one-is-a-complete-translation-invariant-metric]]
supplies the metric structure rather than a normed-space structure.

Adopt as a physical assumption of the pair, additional to P1, P2 and P4 and
valid only for the declared finite-level model of this clause, the following
static electric-dipole coupling. Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the
Axiom of Choice as the choice hypotheses of the cited mathematical suppliers
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

**(i) Declared charged pair and relative coordinate.** Take the declared
two-body Coulomb model of
[[def-nrqm-central-framework-coulomb-and-hydrogen-model]] clause (d): two
distinguishable spinless particles with mass parameters $m_{1},m_{2}>0$ and
opposite charges $-q$ and $+q$, $q>0$ (coulombs), with the relative coordinate
$r=x_{1}-x_{2}$ and the centre-of-mass/relative unitary
$U_{\Phi}$. Work in the relative-coordinate factor $L^{2}(\mathbb
R^{3};\mathbb C)$ of that reading, with Coulomb mass parameter $m=\mu:=m_{1}m_{2}/(m_{1}+m_{2})$, and with units as in
[[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]].

**(ii) Dipole operator.** Let $Q_{j}$, $j=1,2,3$, be the coordinate
multiplication operators on $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb C)$ with maximal
domains $D(Q_{j})=\{\psi:\xi_{j}\psi\in L^{2}\}$ of
[[thm-nrqm-coulomb-atomic-dipole-matrix-element-domain]] clause (a); they are
self-adjoint and proper densely defined. The model's **dipole operator** is
the triple
$$D_{j}:=-q\,Q_{j}\qquad(j=1,2,3),$$
because the dipole of charges $-q$ at $x_{1}$ and $+q$ at $x_{2}$ is
$-qx_{1}+qx_{2}=-qr$: it points from the negative to the positive charge,
opposite to the declared relative coordinate $r=x_{1}-x_{2}$. Each $D_{j}$ is
self-adjoint on $D(Q_{j})$ and has unit $\mathrm{C\,m}$. This is the dipole of
the declared pair in its relative-coordinate reading; no multipole expansion,
no field equation and no coupling to the centre-of-mass motion is assumed.

**(iii) Finite-level truncation.** Fix, as part of the model specification, a
**declared finite-dimensional subspace** $W\subseteq D(H_\kappa)\cap D(Q_{1})\cap D(Q_{2})\cap
D(Q_{3})$ of the relative-coordinate space with $D(H_\kappa)=H^2(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$ and $\dim W=d<\infty$, together
with an orthonormal basis of $W$. The model declares the **compressed dipole
matrix** on $W$,
$$D^{W}_{j}:=\Pi_{W}D_{j}\big|_{W},$$
where $\Pi_{W}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $W$ and the restriction to
$W$ is read in the declared orthonormal basis; $D^{W}_{j}$ is the finite
Hermitian $d\times d$ matrix of the dipole component, with unit
$\mathrm{C\,m}$, and it is bounded with norm at most $\sup_{\psi\in
W,\|\psi\|=1}\|D_{j}\psi\|$. The truncation and the basis are model
assumptions: they are not derived from the Coulomb model, and they replace
the unbounded operator $D_{j}$ by its compression throughout this pair.

**(iv) Static uniform field and interaction operator.** The external datum is
a **uniform static electric field value** $\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\in\mathbb
R^{3}$, read in $\mathrm{V\,m^{-1}}$; it is prescribed, and no Maxwell
equation, source model, propagation or back-reaction is assumed. The
**finite-level static Stark model** is the finite-dimensional operator on $W$
$$H_{S}(\mathbf E_{\rm ext}):=\Pi_{W}H_{\kappa}\big|_{W} -\sum_{j=1}^{3}E_{{\rm ext},j}\,D^{W}_{j},$$
where the energy-domain condition of (iii) makes the compression defined,
and $H_{\kappa}=C_{\mu}$ is the one-centre Coulomb energy operator with
mass parameter $m=\mu$ of the declared model, read on the relative-coordinate
factor through the angular/radial
identification used by the pair. The interaction term has unit
$\mathrm{C\,m\cdot V\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm J$ and is bounded Hermitian on $W$, so
$H_{S}(\mathbf E_{\rm ext})$ is a bounded Hermitian $d\times d$ matrix and
the Kato-Rellich and perturbation statements of the pair apply to it with a
bounded perturbation; this identification of the matrix with the model's
energy on the truncated subspace is a model assumption.

**(v) Scope and explicit exclusion.** Clauses (i)-(iv) are adopted model
assumptions. They assert nothing about a laboratory atom, field or apparatus;
no measured Stark shift is claimed; no transition, absorption or emission
rate is defined; and no time dependence of the field is assumed. In
particular the postulate deliberately does **not** treat the uncompressed
linear potential $-\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\cdot\mathbf D$ as a bounded
perturbation of $H_{\kappa}$. For $\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\ne0$, define this
composite interaction to be the maximal multiplication operator
$$M_{\mathbf E}\psi(\mathbf r):=q\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\cdot\mathbf r\,\psi(\mathbf r),\qquad D(M_{\mathbf E}):=\{\psi\in L^2:(\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\cdot\mathbf r)\psi\in L^2\};$$
it agrees with $-\sum_jE_{{\rm ext},j}D_j$ on the common domain
$\bigcap_jD(D_j)$ and is unbounded because its real multiplier is
unbounded. The common operator domain $D(H_{\kappa})\cap D(M_{\mathbf E})$ contains
$C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. Its lack of a lower bound can be demonstrated
without assuming a full energy-form domain: let $\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\ne0$,
$\widehat e=\mathbf E_{\rm ext}/|\mathbf E_{\rm ext}|$, choose a fixed
support radius $\rho>0$ in metres and normalized
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(B(0,\rho);\mathbb C)$, and for each length $R>\rho$ put
$$\psi_R(\mathbf r):=\varphi(\mathbf r+R\widehat e).$$
Then $\psi_R\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)\subset
D(H_{\kappa})\cap D(M_{\mathbf E})\cap\bigcap_{j=1}^3D(Q_j)$ and
$\|\psi_R\|_2=1$. On this common test domain define the quadratic
expectation
$$\mathcal Q_{\mathbf E_{\rm ext}}[\psi]:=\langle H_{\kappa}\psi,\psi\rangle+\langle M_{\mathbf E}\psi,\psi\rangle.$$
With $\mathbf s=\mathbf r+R\widehat e$, the Coulomb action and the
translation-invariant kinetic expectation give
$$\mathcal Q_{\mathbf E_{\rm ext}}[\psi_R]=\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}\int|\nabla\varphi(\mathbf s)|^2d\mathbf s-\kappa\int\frac{|\varphi(\mathbf s)|^2}{|\mathbf s-R\widehat e|}d\mathbf s+q\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\cdot\int\mathbf s|\varphi(\mathbf s)|^2d\mathbf s-qR|\mathbf E_{\rm ext}|.$$
Here $-\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\cdot\mathbf D=q\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\cdot\mathbf r$
because $\mathbf D=-q\mathbf r$ in the relative-coordinate convention.
For $R>\rho$, the Coulomb integral is finite and at most $1/(R-\rho)$,
the kinetic term is constant, and the other field term apart from
$-qR|\mathbf E_{\rm ext}|$ is independent of $R$. Therefore
$\mathcal Q_{\mathbf E_{\rm ext}}[\psi_R]\to-\infty$ as $R\to\infty$.
This proves unboundedness below of the displayed quadratic expectation on
the common test domain, so no quadratic form bounded below there can agree
with these values; no claim is made about a particular closed-form domain.
The uncompressed static-field
model is outside the scope of every statement of this pair. Only the
compressed finite-level operator of clause (iv) is used.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Let $P_l$ be the Legendre polynomials of
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-legendre-rodrigues-equation]], and for $l\in\mathbb N$ and $0\le m\le l$ define the
function $w_{lm}:(-1,1)\to\mathbb R$ by

$$w_{lm}(t):=(-1)^m(1-t^2)^{m/2}\,\frac{d^m}{dt^m}P_l(t),$$

where $(1-t^2)^{1/2}>0$ denotes the nonnegative square root. Let $\sigma$ be the polar surface measure on
$S^2$ and let the angle coordinates be $\Phi(\theta,\varphi)=(\sin\theta\cos\varphi,\sin\theta\sin\varphi,\cos\theta)$
([[lem-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-integral-in-angle-coordinates]],
[[def-polar-surface-measure-on-the-unit-sphere]]). Then:

(a) each $w_{lm}$ extends continuously to $[-1,1]$, with $w_{lm}(\pm1)=0$ when $m\ge1$, and on $(-1,1)$
it satisfies the associated Legendre equation
$$-\bigl((1-t^2)w_{lm}'\bigr)'+\frac{m^2}{1-t^2}w_{lm}=l(l+1)w_{lm}\qquad(-1<t<1),$$
equivalently $(1-t^2)w_{lm}''-2tw_{lm}'+\Bigl[l(l+1)-\frac{m^2}{1-t^2}\Bigr]w_{lm}=0$;

(b) for fixed $m\ge0$ the functions $w_{lm}$, $l\ge m$, are pairwise orthogonal in $L^2((-1,1),dt)$:
$\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}w_{km}\,dt=0$ for $k\ne l$; moreover $0<\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}^2\,dt<+\infty$;

(c) with $b_{lm}:=\bigl(\int_{-1}^1w_{lm}^2\,dt\bigr)^{-1/2}>0$ and
$$Y_{lm}(\theta,\varphi):=b_{lm}\,w_{lm}(\cos\theta)\,\frac{e^{im\varphi}}{\sqrt{2\pi}}\qquad(l\ge m\ge0),$$
extended by $Y_{l,-m}:=(-1)^m\overline{Y_{lm}}$ for $m\ge1$ (as functions of $(\theta,\varphi)\in(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)$,
$\overline{\ \cdot\ }$ denoting complex conjugation, [[def-complex-exponential]],
[[lem-complex-conjugation-and-modulus-laws]]), one has $|Y_{l,-m}|=|Y_{lm}|$ and
$\overline{Y_{lm}}=(-1)^mY_{l,-m}$ for all $l$ and all $m$ with $|m|\le l$;

(d) the family $\{Y_{lm}:l\ge0,\ -l\le m\le l\}$ is orthonormal in $L^2(S^2,\sigma;\mathbb C)$
([[def-inner-product-space]], [[def-l-p-space-as-a-quotient-by-null-functions]]): for all $(l,m)\ne(l',m')$
with $|m|\le l$, $|m'|\le l'$, the integral $\int_{S^2}Y_{lm}\overline{Y_{l'm'}}\,d\sigma$ equals $0$, and it
equals $1$ when $(l,m)=(l',m')$;

(e) $w_{l0}=P_l$, and $w_{ll}(t)=(-1)^l\frac{(2l)!}{2^l l!}(1-t^2)^{l/2}$.

The functions $Y_{lm}$ are complex-valued $L^2$-functions on the sphere; no physical interpretation as angular
momentum eigenfunctions or spherical harmonics of an atom is asserted.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]). Fix a real parameter $\hbar>0$. Let
$(Y_{lm})_{l\ge0,-l\le m\le l}$ be the complete orthonormal family of $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ constructed in
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-associated-polynomial-normalization]] and
[[thm-nrqm-orbital-and-spin-sphere-onb]], and let
$H:=\operatorname{span}\{Y_{lm}:-l\le m\le l,\ l\in\mathbb N\}$ be its algebraic (finite) span. Define operators
$A$ and $L_z$ on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ by the diagonal lemma
[[lem-nrqm-oscillator-diagonal-adjoint-and-graph-core-lemma]]:

$$D(A):=\Bigl\{F:\sum_{l,m}l^2(l+1)^2\,|\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad AF:=\sum_{l,m}l(l+1)\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm},$$
$$D(L_z):=\Bigl\{F:\sum_{l,m}m^2\,|\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle|^2<\infty\Bigr\},\qquad L_zF:=\sum_{l,m}\hbar m\,\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm},$$

the sums being in the Hilbert-space norm ([[def-hilbert-space]],
[[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]]). Finally, for $F$ in the finite span
$H$ and a chart point $(\theta,\varphi)\in(0,\pi)\times(0,2\pi)$ write $F(\theta,\varphi)$ for the value of $F$
at $\Phi(\theta,\varphi)$ and put

$$(\mathcal S F)(\theta,\varphi):=-\frac1{\sin\theta}\partial_\theta\bigl(\sin\theta\,\partial_\theta F\bigr)(\theta,\varphi) -\frac1{\sin^2\theta}\partial_\varphi^2F(\theta,\varphi),\qquad (\mathcal D F)(\theta,\varphi):=-i\hbar\,\partial_\varphi F(\theta,\varphi),$$

where the partial derivatives are those of [[def-directional-and-partial-derivatives]]. Then:

(a) $A$ and $L_z$ are self-adjoint operators on $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ with the displayed domains; on $Y_{lm}$ they
act by $AY_{lm}=l(l+1)Y_{lm}$ and $L_zY_{lm}=\hbar mY_{lm}$
([[def-self-adjoint-and-normal-endomorphism]]); $A$ is nonnegative, $\langle AF,F\rangle\ge0$, and
$A\mathbf 1=0$;

(b) $H$ is a core of $A$ and of $L_z$: the finite truncations
$F_N:=\sum_{l\le N}\sum_{m}\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm}$ of an element $F$ of $D(A)$ satisfy $F_N\to F$ and
$AF_N\to AF$ in $L^2$, and analogously with $L_z$;

(c) for every $F\in H$ and every chart point with $\sin\theta\ne0$,
$$\mathcal S F(\theta,\varphi)=(AF)(\theta,\varphi),\qquad \mathcal D F(\theta,\varphi)=(L_zF)(\theta,\varphi);$$

(d) for every $l$ the orthogonal projection $P_l$ of $L^2(S^2,\sigma)$ onto the $(2l+1)$-dimensional span of
$Y_{l,-l},\dots,Y_{ll}$ reduces both $A$ and $L_z$ ([[def-orthogonal-projection]]), i.e. $P_lA\subseteq AP_l$
and $P_lL_z\subseteq L_zP_l$; consequently $A$ and $L_z$ commute on the finite span $H$, and for every $F\in D(A)$ with
$\sum_{l,m}\bigl(l(l+1)\hbar m\bigr)^2|\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle|^2<\infty$ one has
$AL_zF=L_zAF=\sum_{l,m}l(l+1)\hbar m\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle Y_{lm}$. Writing $c_{lm}=\langle F,Y_{lm}\rangle$ and $\lambda_l=l(l+1)$, the maximal product domains are $D(AL_z)=\{F\in L^2:\sum_{l,m}(\lambda_l\hbar m)^2|c_{lm}|^2<\infty\}$ and $D(L_zA)=D(A)\cap D(AL_z)$. Thus this is exactly the common domain $D(AL_z)\cap D(L_zA)=D(L_zA)$, while the two maximal product domains need not coincide. The product-weight condition alone does not imply $F\in D(A)$: the vector with coefficients $c_{l0}=1/l$ for $l\ge1$ and all other coefficients zero belongs to $L^2$, has zero product weight, but does not belong to $D(A)$. The product-weight condition is not automatic for all $F\in D(A)\cap D(L_z)$.

The differential expression $\mathcal S$ is evaluated only away from the poles, where the coordinate formulas are
defined; no claim is made about a maximal differential operator on all of $S^2$.

The functions $\sin$ and $\cos$ are differentiable on $\mathbb R$, with
$$(\sin x)'=\cos x,\qquad(\cos x)'=-\sin x.$$
Also $\sin0=0$ and $\cos0=1$.

Let $n\ge1$, let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $f:U\to\mathbb R$ be $C^2$ in the sense of [[def-ck-and-multi-index-notation-in-several-variables]]. Then $\nabla f$ is a $C^1$ field on $U$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], since each of its components $\partial_if$ has continuous first partial derivatives, so its divergence is defined; the **Laplacian** of $f$ is

$$\Delta f:=\operatorname{div}\nabla f=\sum_{i<n}\partial_i\partial_if,$$

with the gradient of [[def-jacobian-matrix-and-gradient]] and the divergence of [[def-divergence-and-curl-of-a-c1-vector-field]]. A $C^2$ function with $\Delta f=0$ on $U$ is called **harmonic** on $U$.

For a $C^2$ map $F=(F_0,\ldots,F_{q-1}):U\to\mathbb R^q$, whose components are $C^2$ by [[def-ck-euclidean-maps-and-diffeomorphisms]], $\Delta F$ is the field whose $i$th coordinate is $\Delta F_i$. In the three-coordinate naming of this page, $\Delta f=\partial_x\partial_xf+\partial_y\partial_yf+\partial_z\partial_zf$ and $\Delta F=(\Delta F_x,\Delta F_y,\Delta F_z)$.

Let $U\subseteq\mathbb R^m$, $a\in U$, $v\in\mathbb R^m$, and $f:U\to\mathbb R^n$. If the line map $t\mapsto f(a+tv)$ is defined near $0$, its derivative at $0$ is the **directional derivative**

$$D_vf(a):=\lim_{t\to0}\frac{f(a+tv)-f(a)}{t}.$$

For a standard basis vector $e_j$ ([[lem-standard-basis-of-f-n]]), $D_{e_j}f(a)$ is the **$j$th partial derivative**, written $\partial_jf(a)$. These are ordinary vector-valued one-variable derivatives in the sense of [[def-vector-valued-derivative-and-integral]].

Let $F$ be a field. Every polynomial in the iterated ring
$F[x_1,\dots,x_n]$ has a unique finite expansion

$$f=\sum_{\mathbf{t}}c_{\mathbf{t}}x^{\mathbf{t}},\qquad x^{\mathbf{t}}:=x_1^{t_1}\cdots x_n^{t_n},$$

over finitely many multi-indices $\mathbf{t}=(t_1,\dots,t_n)\in\mathbb{N}^n$.

For such an index, the scalar $c_{\mathbf{t}}$ is the **coefficient**
$[x^{\mathbf{t}}]f$ of the monomial $x^{\mathbf{t}}$.

The **degree in $x_i$** is the largest $t_i$ with $c_{\mathbf{t}}\ne0$, and the
**total degree** is the largest value of $t_1+\cdots+t_n$ with
$c_{\mathbf{t}}\ne0$. For the zero polynomial, every degree is left undefined.

Evaluation at a point $(a_1,\dots,a_n)\in F^n$ is the iterated substitution
supplied by the universal property of the polynomial ring.

Put $S=k[x_0,\ldots,x_n]$ with total-degree grading. A polynomial is homogeneous of degree $d$ if each occurring monomial has total degree $d$; $0$ is homogeneous in every degree. An ideal $J\subseteq S$ is homogeneous if $F=\sum_dF_d\in J$ implies $F_d\in J$ for every $d$.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice. Let $M$ be a closed linear subspace of a real or complex Hilbert space $H$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). By the orthogonal-decomposition theorem ([[thm-orthogonal-decomposition-by-a-closed-subspace]]) every $x\in H$ has a unique representation

$$x=P_Mx+(x-P_Mx),\qquad P_Mx\in M,\quad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp ,$$

and the **Hilbert orthogonal projection onto $M$** is the map

$$P_M:H\longrightarrow M\subseteq H,\qquad x\longmapsto P_Mx ,$$

assigning to $x$ its unique $M$-component. Its defining properties are therefore

$$P_Mx\in M,\qquad x-P_Mx\in M^\perp\qquad(x\in H),$$

which characterise $P_M$ uniquely: a map with these defining properties must agree with the $M$-component of the unique decomposition of each $x$.

**Agreement with the finite-dimensional projection.** If $V$ is a finite-dimensional inner-product space and $W\subseteq V$ a subspace, then [[thm-finite-dimensional-orthogonal-decomposition]] writes $V=W\oplus W^\perp$ and [[def-orthogonal-projection]] defines $P_Wv$ as the unique $W$-component of $v$; the defining properties displayed above are the same, so they define the same map on a finite-dimensional Hilbert space.

**Range and kernel.** $P_Mx\in M$ for every $x$, and $P_Mm=m$ for $m\in M$ because $m=m+0$ with $0\in M^\perp$; conversely $P_Mx=0$ says exactly that $x=x-0\in M^\perp$. Hence the range of $P_M$ is $M$ and its kernel is $M^\perp$, and $P_M$ is the identity on $M$ and zero on $M^\perp$.

Let $H$ be a real or complex inner-product space ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]), with inner
product linear in the first argument and conjugate-linear in the second, and
with the induced length $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$. The definitions below
do not require completeness. When the term *Hilbert basis* is used, $H$ is
additionally assumed complete ([[def-hilbert-space]]).

**Orthonormal indexed family.** Let $I$ be any set. An indexed family
$(e_i)_{i\in I}$ of vectors of $H$ is **orthonormal** when

$$\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=\delta_{ij}:=\begin{cases}1,&i=j,\\0,&i\ne j,\end{cases} \qquad\text{for all } i,j\in I .$$Because $1\ne 0$ in the scalar field, the family contains no zero vector: $\|e_i\|^2=\langle e_i,e_i\rangle=1$, so $\|e_i\|=1$ for every $i$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]); and the index map is injective, since $e_i=e_j$ with $i\ne j$ would give $0=\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=1$. Thus an orthonormal family is the same thing as an orthonormal set together with a labelling of it, and in the sequel no choice is hidden in passing between the two descriptions. **Orthonormal set.** A subset $S\subseteq H$ is **orthonormal** when every $s\in S$ has $\|s\|=1$ and $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ for all distinct $s,t\in S$. For such an $S$ the family $(e_s)_{s\in S}$ with $e_s:=s$ is orthonormal in the indexed sense, and the image of an orthonormal indexed family is an orthonormal set. Orthogonal means $\langle s,t\rangle=0$ ([[def-orthogonality-and-orthogonal-complement]]). **Independence and unique coefficients.** Let $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ be orthonormal, let $F\subseteq I$ be finite, and let scalars $c_i$ satisfy $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=0$. For each fixed $j\in F$, linearity in the first argument gives$$0=\Bigl\langle \sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i,\;e_j\Bigr\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}c_i\langle e_i,e_j\rangle=c_j ,$$

so every finite subfamily of an orthonormal family is linearly independent. In
particular the coefficients in a finite expansion are unique: if
$\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i=\sum_{i\in F}d_ie_i$, then applying the computation to
$c-d$ gives $c_i=d_i$ for every $i\in F$.

**Closed linear span and completeness.** The **span** of an indexed family is
the set of all finite linear combinations $\sum_{i\in F}c_ie_i$ with $F\subseteq I$
finite and scalars $c_i$; it is the smallest linear subspace of $H$ containing
every $e_i$ ([[def-linear-subspace]]). Its closure in the induced norm is the
**closed linear span** of the family, the smallest closed linear subspace of $H$
containing every $e_i$. The family is **complete**, or is a **complete
orthonormal system**, when its closed linear span is all of $H$. A
**Hilbert basis**, or **orthonormal basis**, of $H$ is a complete orthonormal
family in $H$.

**The empty family.** The span of the empty family is $\{0\}$, which is already
closed, so the empty family is complete exactly when $H=\{0\}$. Thus the zero
Hilbert space always has a Hilbert basis, namely the empty one.

**Not a Hamel basis, and no order is assumed.** A Hilbert basis is a basis only
in the sense of closed linear span: for an infinite-dimensional $H$ the vectors
of $H$ are in general **not** finite linear combinations of a Hilbert basis, and
the expansion of an arbitrary vector is a norm limit of finite partial sums, not
a finite sum. No enumeration, ordering or countability of the index set is part
of the definition; the partial sums are indexed by the finite subsets of $I$,
ordered by inclusion, and that is the convention used on this page.

**Coefficient notation.** For orthonormal $(e_i)_{i\in I}$ and $x\in H$ the
scalars $\langle x,e_i\rangle$ are the **coefficients** of $x$ with respect to
the family. They are well defined for every $x$, without any assumption that
the family is complete.

$$D_{j}:=-q\,Q_{j}\qquad(j=1,2,3),$$

**declared finite-dimensional subspace** $W\subseteq D(H_\kappa)\cap D(Q_{1})\cap D(Q_{2})\cap

with an orthonormal basis of $W$. The model declares the **compressed dipole
matrix** on $W$,
$$D^{W}_{j}:=\Pi_{W}D_{j}\big|_{W},$$
where $\Pi_{W}$ is the orthogonal projection onto $W$ and the restriction to
$W$ is read in the declared orthonormal basis; $D^{W}_{j}$ is the finite
Hermitian $d\times d$ matrix of the dipole component, with unit
$\mathrm{C\,m}$, and it is bounded with norm at most $\sup_{\psi\in

equation, source model, propagation or back-reaction is assumed. The
**finite-level static Stark model** is the finite-dimensional operator on $W$
$$H_{S}(\mathbf E_{\rm ext}):=\Pi_{W}H_{\kappa}\big|_{W} -\sum_{j=1}^{3}E_{{\rm ext},j}\,D^{W}_{j},$$
where the energy-domain condition of (iii) makes the compression defined,
and $H_{\kappa}=C_{\mu}$ is the one-centre Coulomb energy operator with
mass parameter $m=\mu$ of the declared model, read on the relative-coordinate
factor through the angular/radial
identification used by the pair. The interaction term has unit
$\mathrm{C\,m\cdot V\,m^{-1}}=\mathrm J$ and is bounded Hermitian on $W$, so
$H_{S}(\mathbf E_{\rm ext})$ is a bounded Hermitian $d\times d$ matrix and
the Kato-Rellich and perturbation statements of the pair apply to it with a
bounded perturbation; this identification of the matrix with the model's
energy on the truncated subspace is a model assumption.

**(v) Scope and explicit exclusion.** Clauses (i)-(iv) are adopted model

no measured Stark shift is claimed; no transition, absorption or emission
rate is defined; and no time dependence of the field is assumed. In
particular the postulate deliberately does **not** treat the uncompressed
linear potential $-\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\cdot\mathbf D$ as a bounded
perturbation of $H_{\kappa}$. For $\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\ne0$, define this
composite interaction to be the maximal multiplication operator
$$M_{\mathbf E}\psi(\mathbf r):=q\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\cdot\mathbf r\,\psi(\mathbf r),\qquad D(M_{\mathbf E}):=\{\psi\in L^2:(\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\cdot\mathbf r)\psi\in L^2\};$$
it agrees with $-\sum_jE_{{\rm ext},j}D_j$ on the common domain
$\bigcap_jD(D_j)$ and is unbounded because its real multiplier is
unbounded. The common operator domain $D(H_{\kappa})\cap D(M_{\mathbf E})$ contains
$C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)$. Its lack of a lower bound can be demonstrated
without assuming a full energy-form domain: let $\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\ne0$,
$\widehat e=\mathbf E_{\rm ext}/|\mathbf E_{\rm ext}|$, choose a fixed
support radius $\rho>0$ in metres and normalized
$\varphi\in C_c^\infty(B(0,\rho);\mathbb C)$, and for each length $R>\rho$ put
$$\psi_R(\mathbf r):=\varphi(\mathbf r+R\widehat e).$$
Then $\psi_R\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R^3;\mathbb C)\subset
D(H_{\kappa})\cap D(M_{\mathbf E})\cap\bigcap_{j=1}^3D(Q_j)$ and
$\|\psi_R\|_2=1$. On this common test domain define the quadratic
expectation
$$\mathcal Q_{\mathbf E_{\rm ext}}[\psi]:=\langle H_{\kappa}\psi,\psi\rangle+\langle M_{\mathbf E}\psi,\psi\rangle.$$
With $\mathbf s=\mathbf r+R\widehat e$, the Coulomb action and the
translation-invariant kinetic expectation give
$$\mathcal Q_{\mathbf E_{\rm ext}}[\psi_R]=\frac{\hbar^2}{2\mu}\int|\nabla\varphi(\mathbf s)|^2d\mathbf s-\kappa\int\frac{|\varphi(\mathbf s)|^2}{|\mathbf s-R\widehat e|}d\mathbf s+q\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\cdot\int\mathbf s|\varphi(\mathbf s)|^2d\mathbf s-qR|\mathbf E_{\rm ext}|.$$
Here $-\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\cdot\mathbf D=q\mathbf E_{\rm ext}\cdot\mathbf r$
because $\mathbf D=-q\mathbf r$ in the relative-coordinate convention.
For $R>\rho$, the Coulomb integral is finite and at most $1/(R-\rho)$,
the kinetic term is constant, and the other field term apart from
$-qR|\mathbf E_{\rm ext}|$ is independent of $R$. Therefore
$\mathcal Q_{\mathbf E_{\rm ext}}[\psi_R]\to-\infty$ as $R\to\infty$.
This proves unboundedness below of the displayed quadratic expectation on
the common test domain, so no quadratic form bounded below there can agree
with these values; no claim is made about a particular closed-form domain.

**(a) Dimensions.** Write $\ell$, $\tau$, $\mu$, $\vartheta$ for the four independent dimension symbols of length, duration, mass and electric charge. A **dimension** is an element of $\mathbb Z^{4}$, written $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$; products and inverses of dimensions are componentwise addition and negation, and the dimensionless dimension $\ell^{0}\tau^{0}\mu^{0}\vartheta^{0}$ is abbreviated $1$. The conventions assign to each quantity of the framework a dimension $[X]$, subject to $[XY]=[X][Y]$, $[X/Y]=[X][Y]^{-1}$ and $[dX/du]=[X][u]^{-1}$, with sums meaningful only between quantities of equal dimension, in which case the sum carries that dimension. These are consistency requirements on the conventions, not laws of nature.

**(b) Reference units.** The **metre** (m), **second** (s), **kilogram** (kg) and **coulomb** (C) are the reference units of length, duration, mass and charge; a quantity of dimension $\ell^{a}\tau^{b}\mu^{c}\vartheta^{d}$ is expressed in the unit $\mathrm m^{a}\mathrm s^{b}\mathrm kg^{c}\mathrm C^{d}$. Coordinates of an inertial frame are read with the time coordinate $t$ in seconds, $[t]=\tau$, and the spatial coordinates $x_{i}$ in metres, $[x_{i}]=\ell$; slice distances of the arena are read in metres.

**(c) Defining constants of the current SI.** The framework keeps $\hbar$ explicit. In the current SI the constants $h$, $c$ and $e$ are exact defining constants, with the values $h=6{,}626\,070\,15\times10^{-34}$ J s, $c=2{,}99792458\times10^{8}$ m s$^{-1}$ and $e=1{,}602\,176\,634\times10^{-19}$ C, and $\hbar:=h/(2\pi)$; the vacuum permeability $\mu_{0}$ is experimentally determined and $\varepsilon_{0}:=(\mu_{0}c^{2})^{-1}$. These are unit-convention statements of the SI, not measurements reported by this framework; $c$ enters the framework only through the separate radiation assumptions adopted on their own pages, not in the nonrelativistic spacetime of [[def-nrqm-framework-newtonian-spacetime]].

1. State quantities: a position wave function of a system with $d$ spatial dimensions and $r$ internal components is an almost-everywhere equivalence class in $L^{2}(\mathbb R^{d};\mathbb C^{r})$ with dimension $\ell^{-d/2}$, its norm $\|\psi\|$ is dimensionless, and an abstract normalized state and the density operators of the state postulate are dimensionless.
2. Probability: the outcome probability $\mu(B)$ of the observable postulate is a dimensionless number; a position density $|\psi|^{2}$ has dimension $\ell^{-d}$; a momentum wave function normalized against $\mathrm d^{d}p$ has dimension $(\mu\ell\tau^{-1})^{-d/2}$; an amplitude for a finite outcome is a dimensionless complex number, while an amplitude read against a detector coordinate carries the square-root of the inverse of the detector measure.
3. Frame parameters ([[def-nrqm-framework-galilei-transformations]]): $[b]=\tau$, $[a_{i}]=\ell$, $[v_{i}]=\ell\tau^{-1}$ and $[R_{ij}]=1$.
4. Mechanical quantities: action $[\hbar]=\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; energy and the Hamiltonian eigenvalues $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$; momentum $\mu\ell\tau^{-1}$; position components $\ell$; angular momentum and spin $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-1}$; mass $\mu$; velocity of a free spinless model $\ell\tau^{-1}$; force $\mu\ell\tau^{-2}$; a real potential energy $\mu\ell^{2}\tau^{-2}$.
5. Probability current: $j$ has dimension $\ell^{1-d}\tau^{-1}$; it is a probability flux, not a charge flux.
6. Electric quantities of the model parameters: charge has dimension $\vartheta$; a magnetic moment has dimension $\ell^{2}\vartheta\tau^{-1}$, equivalently $\mathrm A\,\mathrm m^{2}=\mathrm J\,\mathrm T^{-1}$, and a gyromagnetic parameter $\gamma$ in the relation $\boldsymbol\mu=\gamma\mathbf S$ has dimension $\mu^{-1}\vartheta$, equivalently $\mathrm s^{-1}\mathrm T^{-1}$; these quantities appear only in the model assumptions that introduce them.
7. Statistical quantities: a mean has the dimension of its outcome coordinate, a variance the square of it and a standard deviation it; a mean, variance or higher moment exists only when the corresponding moment of the outcome probability is finite, so a symbolic average is not a number unless that integrability is established. Angles and phases are dimensionless under the radian convention.
8. Quantities of later extension assumptions - radiation frequencies and energies, electric dipole moments, cross sections, temperatures and entropies - are declared with their dimensions and units by the items that introduce those assumptions, under the rules fixed here; they are not part of the present list.

**(e) Conventions only.** No numerical value of any model parameter is fixed by this item: no mass, charge, spin label, potential or measured constant is asserted, and natural-unit shorthand (for example setting $\hbar=1$ or $c=1$) is read as an abbreviation for the corresponding SI-dimensioned statement with the constant restored.

For a preparation $\rho$, that is a state $\rho\in D(H)$ of [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-pure-mixed-states-and-purity]], the **outcome law** of the pair $(A,u_A)$ in the preparation $\rho$ is the assignment
$$\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B):=\operatorname{tr}\bigl(\rho\,E_A(B)\bigr)\qquad(B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel}),$$
the reading of clause (ii) of P2; for the pure preparation $[\psi]$ of a unit vector $\psi$ it is $\mu^{A}_{\psi}(B)=\|E_A(B)\psi\|^{2}$, which depends only on the ray by [[def-nrqm-state-geometry-state-vectors-and-rays]]. The law is a probability measure on the Borel sets by [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (b), and it is affine in the preparation: for a statistical mixture $\sum_nw_n\rho_n$ one has $\mu^{A}_{\sum_nw_n\rho_n}=\sum_nw_n\mu^{A}_{\rho_n}$ by [[lem-nrqm-observables-outcome-law-affinity-and-trace-norm-continuity]] clause (b).

**(c) Outcome sets and exact values.** A declared finite-resolution outcome of the quantity is a Borel set $B$; its probability in the preparation $\rho$ is $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)$, and a "value in $B$" is read only through this number. The reading of an **exact value** $\lambda$ is the singleton $B=\{\lambda\}$, with probability $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\{\lambda\})$; by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-measure-atoms-and-eigenvalues]] clauses (a) and (b) this number is zero for every preparation unless $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue of $A$, and when $\lambda$ is an eigenvalue it is the total weight of the eigenspace. In particular the model provides no normalizable eigenvector at a non-eigenvalue of $A$, and an exact value of a quantity with no eigenvalues is an idealization outside the assignment, in the sense of clause (iii) of P2.

**(d) Spectral support.** The outcomes of the observable lie in its spectrum: with $\sigma(A)$ the spectrum of [[def-resolvent-and-spectrum-of-a-closed-unbounded-operator]], one has $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B)=\mu^{A}_{\rho}(B\cap\sigma(A))$ and $\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\sigma(A))=1$ for every preparation by [[lem-nrqm-observables-spectral-support-and-outcome-law]] clause (b). This is the precise reading of the statement that the result of a measurement lies in the spectrum of the observable.

**(e) Moments.** The **mean** and the **variance** of the outcome law in a preparation are the numbers $\int\lambda\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ and $\int(\lambda-m)^{2}\,d\mu^{A}_{\rho}(\lambda)$ with $m$ the mean, read in the declared unit $u_A$ and its square respectively; they exist only under the integrability hypotheses of [[lem-nrqm-observables-moments-and-variance]], which also supplies the formulas in terms of $A$ and the state. For a pure preparation of a unit vector $\psi\in D(A)$ the mean and the second moment are $\langle A\psi,\psi\rangle$ and $\|A\psi\|^{2}$; membership of $\psi$ in $D(A)$ or in $D(A^{2})$ is a genuine hypothesis and is not asserted for an arbitrary preparation.

**(f) Unsharp finite outcomes are separate.** Clause (iv) of P2 permits a finite family of bounded effects $F_a$ with $0\le F_a\le I$ and $\sum_aF_a=I$ and outcome probabilities $\operatorname{tr}(\rho F_a)$ as an operational description of a finite-resolution apparatus. That extension is tied to an apparatus instrument and is developed, together with state updates, on the measurement-and-instruments page; this definition fixes only the sharp outcome law of clause (b) and makes no claim that every laboratory procedure realizes it.

**(g) Status.** Clauses (a)-(f) record the readings of P1 and P2 in the vocabulary of this page and fix the terminology used by the later pages of the category. They adopt no physical assumption beyond P1 and P2 and the choice hypotheses of the spectral theorem, assert no dynamics, no joint measurement of several observables, no detector realization and no empirical result, and make no claim that any physical system is exactly described by an assigned pair $(A,u_A)$. The additive additivity, support, atom and moment statements cited are mathematical consequences proved in the cited items; their physical reading is exactly the reading of P2 fixed here.

Adopt as physical assumptions of the framework, for systems in the declared massive-matter sector, the following statements about states and their composition. Assume throughout the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]), which is the choice hypothesis of the mathematical suppliers cited below.

**(i) State space.** To each physical system of the sector the model assigns a complex Hilbert space $H$ that is nonzero and separable: a complex Hilbert space in the sense of [[def-hilbert-space]] which admits a sequence whose range is dense in $H$, so that the hypothesis of [[thm-separable-hilbert-space-has-a-countable-orthonormal-basis]] holds and $H$ has a finite or countable orthonormal basis. The assignment of a Hilbert space to a physical system is a model assumption; the linear structure used to combine descriptions mathematically is not an empirical claim. The physical system to which $H$ is assigned, and the sector in which the assignment is made, are declared with it.

**(ii) Pure preparations.** A **pure preparation** of the system is a unit ray $[\psi]=\{z\psi:z\in\mathbb C\setminus\{0\}\}$ of a vector $\psi\in H$ with $\|\psi\|=1$; that is, two nonzero vectors describe the same pure preparation exactly when they differ by a nonzero complex factor. The zero vector is not a state and no preparation is assigned to it: the normalization $\|\psi\|=1$ is part of the assignment. The ray allows arbitrary nonzero rescaling; between unit representatives the factor has modulus one and is a **global phase**, which has no observable consequence (P2). The rank-one operator $T_{\psi,\psi}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-rank-one-operator-calculus]] is the density operator associated with the ray of $\psi$.

**(iii) General preparations and mixing.** A general preparation of the system is a **density operator**: a self-adjoint positive trace-class operator $\rho$ on $H$ with $\operatorname{tr}\rho=1$ ([[def-trace-class-operator]], [[def-trace-of-a-trace-class-operator]], [[lem-nrqm-composites-density-and-scalar-spectral-probability]] clause (a)). Pure preparations are the special case $\rho=T_{\psi,\psi}$ with $\|\psi\|=1$. A **statistical mixture** of preparations $\rho_{n}$ with weights $w_{n}\ge0$, $\sum_{n}w_{n}=1$, is the trace-norm convergent sum $\rho=\sum_{n}w_{n}\rho_{n}$ as follows directly in the trace-class Banach space ([[thm-trace-class-is-a-two-sided-banach-operator-ideal]]): each density has trace norm one, so $\sum_n\|w_n\rho_n\|_1=1$ gives trace-norm convergence. Every partial sum is positive; operator-norm convergence preserves its nonnegative quadratic forms, and continuity of trace gives $\operatorname{tr}\rho=\sum_nw_n=1$ ([[thm-trace-is-absolutely-convergent-and-basis-independent]]). Thus the limit is again a density operator, without requiring the components to be orthogonal pure states. The weights are a classical preparation uncertainty and are not amplitudes. Distinct weighted ensembles of pure states may define the same $\rho$.

**(iv) Composition.** Two independent distinguishable subsystems with state spaces $H_{A}$ and $H_{B}$ are composed by the completed Hilbert tensor product $H_{A}\widehat\otimes H_{B}$ of [[lem-nrqm-composites-hilbert-tensor-construction]]. Product preparations $\psi_{A}\otimes\psi_{B}$ are the special case of preparations in which each subsystem has its own specified preparation; general composite preparations are linear combinations and mixtures and need not factor. A quantity of subsystem $A$ alone is represented on the composite by an operator of the form $A\otimes I_{B}$ and a quantity of $B$ alone by $I_{A}\otimes B$, in the sense of [[lem-nrqm-composites-bounded-tensor-maps]] (bounded case; unbounded local operators are treated where they occur). The existence of the completed tensor product is mathematics; the assignment of that product to a composite physical system is the physical assumption here.

**(v) Restrictions that are separate assumptions.** Restrictions of the state space by superselection rules, identical-particle symmetry sectors, and the replacement of the tensor product by more general algebraic structures are not consequences of the clauses above: where such a restriction is used it is adopted separately, and the identical-species sectors are the subject of the postulate P6 of this page.

**(vi) Status.** Clauses (i)-(v) are adopted assumptions of the model within its declared sector. They are not derived from experiment, and they do not assert that a physical system is exactly described by such a Hilbert space; no numerical measurement is recorded. The compatibility of the framework with observation is a question about fully specified models and reported data, in the sense of P7.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), let $c$ be a nonzero real and write
$cE := \{\, cx : x \in E \,\}$ for $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$, where
$(cx)_i := cx_i$. Then:

1. $\lambda_n^*(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\,\lambda_n^*(E)$ for every subset $E$, the
   product being defined in $\overline{\mathbb{R}}$ because $|c|^{\,n} > 0$;
2. $E$ is Lebesgue measurable if and only if $cE$ is;
3. $\lambda_n(cE) = |c|^{\,n}\lambda_n(E)$ for every Lebesgue measurable $E$.

At $c = -1$ the map is reflection in the origin and $|c|^{\,n} = 1$, so it
preserves outer measure, measurability and measure. The value $c = 0$ is
excluded because $0E$ is $\{0\}$ or $\varnothing$ and carries no information
about $E$.

derivations.claim: [Domain and factorisation] Clause (a) is [F1]: each bound state lies in every $D(X_{i})$, so $D_{q}\psi_{nlm}=-q_{\mathrm{el}}Q_q\psi_{nlm}$ is defined and the matrix element is absolutely convergent. For clause (b), [F1] gives the factorisation $\langle\psi_{n'l'm'},D_{q}\psi_{nlm}\rangle=-q_{\mathrm{el}}\langle\psi_{n'l'm'},Q_{q}\psi_{nlm}\rangle$ with the displayed radial and angular factors.

[Angular degree and weight] Let $\mathcal H:=h_{lm}$, the homogeneous harmonic representative of $Y_{lm}$ from [F2]. Write $Q_q=\sum_{i=1}^{3}a_{q,i}x_i$, where $a_{0,i}=\delta_{i3}$ and $a_{\pm,i}=(\delta_{i1}\pm i\delta_{i2})/\sqrt2$; these coefficients match exactly $Q_{\pm}=(x_1\pm ix_2)/\sqrt2$. If $l\ge1$, put $G_q:=(\sum_i a_{q,i}\partial_i\mathcal H)/(2l+1)$; since $\mathcal H$ is harmonic, partial derivatives commute with $\Delta$, so $G_q$ is harmonic homogeneous of degree $l-1$. If $l=0$, put $G_q:=0$. The product rule gives $\Delta(Q_q\mathcal H)=2\sum_i a_{q,i}\partial_i\mathcal H$. For $l\ge1$, [F2] gives $\Delta(r^2G_q)=(4(l-1)+6)G_q=(4l+2)G_q=2\sum_i a_{q,i}\partial_i\mathcal H$; for $l=0$ both sides are zero. Thus $R_q:=Q_q\mathcal H-r^2G_q$ is harmonic homogeneous of degree $l+1$. Restricting to $S^2$, where $r^2=1$, yields $Q_qY_{lm}=R_q|_{S^2}+G_q|_{S^2}$ when $l\ge1$ and only the first term when $l=0$. By [F2], this lies in $V_{l+1}\oplus V_{l-1}$ (with $V_{-1}=\{0\}$), so its pairing with $Y_{l'm'}$ vanishes if $l'\notin\{l-1,l+1\}$. The product $F:=Q_qY_{lm}$ is consequently in the finite span $H$. On the chart, [F2] and the product rule give $\partial_{\varphi}F=iqF+imF=i(m+q)F$: indeed $\partial_{\varphi}Q_q=iqQ_q$, while $\partial_{\varphi}Y_{lm}=imY_{lm}$ follows from $L_zY_{lm}=\hbar mY_{lm}$ and $L_z=-i\hbar\partial_{\varphi}$. Hence $L_zF=\hbar(m+q)F$. If $m'\ne m+q$, self-adjointness of $L_z$ and $L_zY_{l'm'}=\hbar m'Y_{l'm'}$ imply $(m+q-m')\hbar\langle F,Y_{l'm'}\rangle=0$, so $\langle F,Y_{l'm'}\rangle=0$. Since the reversed angular pairing in the Statement is its complex conjugate, it vanishes under the same conditions. This proves the claimed degree and component-dependent weight restrictions.

[Necessary conditions] Clause (c) restates step 2.1: $m'-m=q\in\{0,\pm1\}$ and $l'-l\in\{-1,+1\}$ are necessary for a nonvanishing matrix element; the radial factor is not controlled by [F2], so no nonvanishing statement is made for an allowed angular pair, and no probability or rate is defined.

[Parity on the actual coordinate domains] By [F6], $\Pi_{\mathrm{par}}$ is a unitary involution on $L^2$. For any $u\in L^2$, reflection invariance and $Q_q(-x)=-Q_q(x)$ from [F3] give $\int|Q_q(x)|^2|u(-x)|^2dx=\int|Q_q(-x)|^2|u(x)|^2dx=\int|Q_q(x)|^2|u(x)|^2dx$, allowing infinite values. Consequently $\Pi_{\mathrm{par}}D(Q_q)=D(Q_q)$ and, on that domain, $\Pi_{\mathrm{par}}Q_q\Pi_{\mathrm{par}}=-Q_q$. Also [F3] gives $\Pi_{\mathrm{par}}\psi_{nlm}=(-1)^l\psi_{nlm}$ because its radial factor depends on $|x|$ only. Now let $u\in D(Q_q)$ and $v\in L^2$ satisfy $\Pi_{\mathrm{par}}u=\sigma u$, $\Pi_{\mathrm{par}}v=\sigma'v$ with real $\sigma,\sigma'\in\{-1,1\}$. Unitarity and the defined-domain identity give $\langle v,Q_qu\rangle=\langle\Pi_{\mathrm{par}}v,\Pi_{\mathrm{par}}Q_qu\rangle=-\sigma\sigma'\langle v,Q_qu\rangle$. A nonzero pairing therefore forces $\sigma\sigma'=-1$. The charge $q_{\mathrm{el}}>0$ preserves nonvanishing when $Q_q$ is replaced by $D_q=-q_{\mathrm{el}}Q_q$. Applying this to the bound states, whose input domains are supplied by [F1], gives $(-1)^{l'}=-(-1)^l$ and proves (d).

[Compression] The finite span $W$ of the selected bound states lies in every $D(X_i)$ and hence in every $D(Q_q)=D(D_q)$ by [F1] and linearity of those domains. Thus $D_q^W=\Pi_WD_q|_W$ is defined on all $W$. For $w,w'\in W$, the reversed-pairing identity of [F4] gives $\langle w',D_q^Ww\rangle=\langle w',D_qw\rangle$, which is exactly the valid display of (e). In the selected orthonormal basis the actual coordinate entry is $\langle D_qw_j,w_i\rangle$, the conjugate of $\langle w_i,D_qw_j\rangle$; either vanishes exactly when the other does. Therefore each matrix entry inherits the uncompressed angular and parity vanishing conditions from steps 2.1 and 3.2, including the complex spherical components, proving (e).

[Scope and assembly] Steps 1.1 and 2.1 prove (a) and (b), step 3.1 proves (c), step 3.2 proves (d) and step 4.1 proves (e). Only matrix elements of the declared model's dipole components entered; no transition probability, rate, lineshape or observed spectrum was formed, and the neglected higher-order terms are recorded as outside the theorem, which is (f).

clause (a). Assume the Axioms of Countable Choice and of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]) and the density hypothesis:
$\nu_{b}=J_{b}\lambda$ for some $J_{b}\in L^{1}(\lambda)$ with $J_{b}=0$
$\lambda$-almost everywhere on $\mathbb R\setminus(0,\Lambda]$, continuous at
$\Delta$. Then:

(a) (resonant limit) if $0<\Delta<\Lambda$ and $J_{b}(\Delta)>0$, then

read in $\mathrm{s^{-1}}$ by the unit convention of the model (the interaction
term is read in joules), as the model's reading of the limit in (a); the
identification of the mode density $J_{b}$, the cutoff $\Lambda$ or the
coupling $\eta_{0}$ with laboratory data is a tested identification with
uncertainty under P7
([[post-nrqm-framework-preparation-and-apparatus]]);

coefficient per unit time. They assert no exact exponential decay of any
population, no lifetime or linewidth, no weak-coupling, Markov or

decay constant.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix $\hbar>0$ and let $\alpha>0$, let
$\mathfrak h=\operatorname{ran}M_{\Pi}\subseteq L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb
C^{3})$ be the transverse space with $\varepsilon(k)=\alpha|k|$ of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-transverse-continuum-free-fock-hamiltonian]],
let $\Lambda>0$, let $g_{1},\dots,g_{J}\in\mathfrak h$ ($J\ge1$) satisfy
$$\operatorname{supp}g_{j}\subseteq\{k:\ 0<\varepsilon(k)\le\Lambda\},\qquad \frac{g_{j}}{\sqrt\varepsilon}\in\mathfrak h ,$$
let $\eta_{0}\in\mathbb R$ and let $c_{1},\dots,c_{J}\in\mathbb C$ with
$$M:=\sum_{j=1}^{J}c_{j}g_{j}\in\mathfrak h .$$
Fix $\Delta\in\mathbb R$ and define the finite Borel measure
$$\nu_{b}(B):=\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}\mathbf 1_{B}\bigl(\varepsilon(k)\bigr) \|M(k)\|_{\mathbb C^{3}}^{2}\,d^{3}k,\qquad K_{t}(x):=\frac{1}{\hbar^{2}t}\Bigl|\int_{0}^{t}e^{ixs/\hbar}\,ds\Bigr|^{2}\ \ (t>0),$$
and the vector-valued function
$$A_{b}(k,t):=-\frac{i\eta_{0}}{\hbar}M(k)\int_{0}^{t} e^{i(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)s/\hbar}\,ds\qquad(t\ge0).$$
Clause (a) includes $M=0$ and every real $\eta_0$, including zero. Clauses (b)-(e) concern the normalized law when $M\ne0$; no nonzero assumption on $\eta_0$ is required. Then:

(a) (factorisation) for every $t>0$ and almost every $k\in\mathbb R^{3}$,
$$|A_{b}(k,t)|^{2}=\eta_{0}^{2}\,t\,K_{t}\bigl(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta\bigr) \|M(k)\|_{\mathbb C^{3}}^{2},$$
and consequently
$\|A_{b}(\cdot,t)\|_{\mathfrak h}^{2}=\eta_{0}^{2}t\int_{\mathbb R}
K_{t}(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_{b}(E)$;

(b) (normalisation) if $M\ne0$, then for every $t>0$ the denominator
$\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_{b}(E)$ is finite and strictly positive,
so
$$P_{t}(B):=\frac{\int_{B}K_{t}(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_{b}(E)} {\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_{b}(E)}$$
defines a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$ with
$P_{t}(\mathbb R\setminus(0,\Lambda])=0$;

(c) (concentration) if $\nu_{b}=J_{b}\lambda$ for some $J_{b}\in
L^{1}(\lambda)$ with $J_{b}=0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere on
$\mathbb R\setminus(0,\Lambda]$, if $J_{b}$ is continuous at some $\Delta$ with
$0<\Delta<\Lambda$ and $J_{b}(\Delta)>0$, and if $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is
continuous and bounded, then
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb R}f\,dP_{t}=f(\Delta);$$

(d) (positivity) if $\nu_{b}=J_{b}\lambda$ with $J_{b}\ge0$
$\lambda$-almost everywhere and $J_{b}>0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere on a
Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ of positive Lebesgue measure, then
$P_{t}(B)>0$ for every $t>0$;

(e) (tail concentration) under the hypotheses of (c), for every $\delta>0$,
$\lim_{t\to\infty}P_{t}\bigl(\{E:|E-\Delta|\ge\delta\}\bigr)=0$.

No dynamics, transition probability, rate, decay or physical identification is
asserted; the lemma computes an explicit kernel, its normalised push-forward
law and that law's limit.

the units of [[def-nrqm-framework-quantities-and-units]]. Assume the Axioms of

[[def-axiom-of-choice]]).

**(b) Declared level pair and transition energy.** A **declared level pair**
$(a,b)$ of the model is an ordered pair of orthonormal eigenvectors $v_{a},
v_{b}\in\mathbb C^{d}$ of the compressed matter energy $H_{a}$
([[def-orthonormal-family-complete-orthonormal-system-and-hilbert-basis]],
[[def-inner-product-space]]). Its **transition energy** is
$\Delta:=E_{a}-E_{b}$, read in joules; the pair is **upward** when
$\Delta>0$, meaning level $a$ lies above level $b$ in the model's energy
ordering.

**(c) Dipole coefficients and single-vertex photon density.** For an upward
declared level pair $(a,b)$ and the couplings $D_j^{\mathrm{ch}},g_{j},\eta_{0}$ of
[[def-nrqm-light-matter-framework-finite-level-coupled-model]] clauses (c),(d),
the model's **dipole coefficients** are the complex numbers
$$c_{j}:=\bigl\langle D_j^{\mathrm{ch}}v_{a},\,v_{b}\bigr\rangle_{\mathbb C^{d}} \qquad(j=1,\dots,J),$$
the model's **single-vertex mode vector** is
$$M:=\sum_{j=1}^{J}c_{j}\,g_{j}\in\mathfrak h,$$
and the model's **single-vertex photon density** is the finite Borel measure on
$\mathbb R$
$$\nu_{b}(B):=\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}\mathbf 1_{B}\bigl(\varepsilon(k)\bigr)\, \|M(k)\|_{\mathbb C^{3}}^{2}\,d^{3}k,\qquad B\subseteq\mathbb R\ \text{Borel},$$
read in the model's units and supported in $(0,\Lambda]$. The pairing is linear in its first argument and conjugate-linear in its
second. Thus $c_j$ is the actual coefficient of $v_b$ in $D_j^{\mathrm{ch}}v_a$,
and Hermiticity gives $\langle D_j^{\mathrm{ch}}v_b,v_a\rangle=\overline{c_j}$.
These are exactly the coefficients of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-golden-rule-coefficient-approximate-identity]]
clause (c), with no conjugation or change of the transverse mode vectors;
its mode vector and measure are the present $M$ and $\nu_b$.

**(d) Single-vertex emission vector and coefficient.** For $t\ge0$ the model's
**single-vertex emission vector** is the element of $\mathfrak h$
$$A_{b}(\cdot,t):\quad k\mapsto-\frac{i\eta_{0}}{\hbar}M(k) \int_{0}^{t}e^{i(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)s/\hbar}\,ds ,$$
and the model's **single-vertex emission coefficient** is
$$\gamma_{b}(t):=\|A_{b}(\cdot,t)\|_{\mathfrak h}^{2}.$$
The vector and the coefficient are **defined model quantities**: the model
assigns them through this clause and through the cutoff dipole mathematics, and
they are not asserted to be the exact probability of any measurement of the
model. In particular $\gamma_{b}(t)$ is dimensionless and is not a rate; the
reading of a rate coefficient requires a separate limit statement, which is not
part of this definition.

$t>0$ and $M\ne0$ the model's **normalised single-vertex photon-energy law** is
the Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$
$$P_{b,t}(B):=\frac{\int_{B}K_{t}(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_{b}(E)} {\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_{b}(E)},\qquad K_{t}(x):=\frac{1}{\hbar^{2}t}\Bigl|\int_{0}^{t}e^{ixs/\hbar}\,ds\Bigr|^{2},$$
whose denominator is finite and strictly positive by
[[lem-nrqm-light-matter-first-order-photon-energy-law]] clause (b). This
probability law is defined independently of $\eta_0$, including $\eta_0=0$.
Its amplitude-based preparation reading additionally requires $A_b(\cdot,t)\ne0$.
For $t>0$ and $M\ne0$, this is equivalent to $\eta_0\ne0$, since
$\|A_b(\cdot,t)\|^2=\eta_0^2t\int K_t(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_b(E)$ and the integral
is positive. Under this condition the **declared single-vertex
one-photon preparation** is the unit vector $v_{b}\otimes(A_{b}(\cdot,t)/\|A_{b}(\cdot,t)\|_{\mathfrak h})$
of $\mathbb C^{d}\otimes\mathfrak h\subseteq\mathbb C^{d}\otimes
F(\mathfrak h)$, and for a Borel window $B\subseteq[0,\infty)$ the declared
ideal energy-window detector of window $B$ of
[[def-nrqm-photons-framework-ideal-counting-and-detection-model]] clause (c)
has the Born probability $P_{b,t}(B)$ in that preparation, because the energy
law of a unit one-photon vector $f$ is the push-forward of
$\|f(k)\|_{\mathbb C^{3}}^{2}d^{3}k$ under $k\mapsto\varepsilon(k)$
([[def-nrqm-photons-framework-radiation-sector-and-quantum-assignments]] clause
(e)). When $\eta_0=0$, $A_b(\cdot,t)=0$ and no preparation obtained by
normalizing that emission amplitude is declared; the formal law $P_{b,t}$
remains the probability measure defined above. A **detected photon energy** is therefore a spectral reading of the
assigned free-field energy observable $(H_{f},\mathrm J)$, not a sharp energy
of a normalisable state and not a quantum number of the model's mode labels.

**(f) Scope.** Clauses (b)-(e) fix the model's spectral vocabulary. They assert

of $\nu_{b}$, and a point mass at $\Delta$ is only the idealisation proved as a
limit in [[lem-nrqm-light-matter-first-order-photon-energy-law]] clause (c).

declared ideal window, no efficiency, no background, no sampling model, no
count and no measurement record; the identification of a laboratory
spectrometer with a declared window is a tested identification with uncertainty
under P7. The single-vertex quantities of clauses (d)-(e) are conditional model
data; their relation to the model's exact outcome probabilities is a separate
proved statement.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be a measure space and let
$f:X\to[0,+\infty]$ be measurable. The **measure with density $f$ relative
to $\mu$** is the measure
$$f\,d\mu:\mathcal A\to[0,+\infty],\qquad (f\,d\mu)(A):=\int_A f\,d\mu,$$
whose measure property is supplied by
[[thm-indefinite-integral-of-a-nonnegative-function-is-a-measure]].

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice and the Axiom of Choice
([[def-countable-choice]], [[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Fix $\hbar>0$ and let $\alpha>0$, let
$\mathfrak h=\operatorname{ran}M_{\Pi}\subseteq L^{2}(\mathbb R^{3};\mathbb
C^{3})$ be the transverse space with $\varepsilon(k)=\alpha|k|$ of
[[thm-nrqm-fock-and-equilibrium-transverse-continuum-free-fock-hamiltonian]],
let $\Lambda>0$, let $g_{1},\dots,g_{J}\in\mathfrak h$ ($J\ge1$) satisfy
$$\operatorname{supp}g_{j}\subseteq\{k:\ 0<\varepsilon(k)\le\Lambda\},\qquad \frac{g_{j}}{\sqrt\varepsilon}\in\mathfrak h ,$$
let $\eta_{0}\in\mathbb R$ and let $c_{1},\dots,c_{J}\in\mathbb C$ with
$$M:=\sum_{j=1}^{J}c_{j}g_{j}\in\mathfrak h .$$
Fix $\Delta\in\mathbb R$ and define the finite Borel measure
$$\nu_{b}(B):=\int_{\mathbb R^{3}}\mathbf 1_{B}\bigl(\varepsilon(k)\bigr) \|M(k)\|_{\mathbb C^{3}}^{2}\,d^{3}k,\qquad K_{t}(x):=\frac{1}{\hbar^{2}t}\Bigl|\int_{0}^{t}e^{ixs/\hbar}\,ds\Bigr|^{2}\ \ (t>0),$$
and the vector-valued function
$$A_{b}(k,t):=-\frac{i\eta_{0}}{\hbar}M(k)\int_{0}^{t} e^{i(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta)s/\hbar}\,ds\qquad(t\ge0).$$
Clause (a) includes $M=0$ and every real $\eta_0$, including zero. Clauses (b)-(e) concern the normalized law when $M\ne0$; no nonzero assumption on $\eta_0$ is required. Then:

(a) (factorisation) for every $t>0$ and almost every $k\in\mathbb R^{3}$,
$$|A_{b}(k,t)|^{2}=\eta_{0}^{2}\,t\,K_{t}\bigl(\varepsilon(k)-\Delta\bigr) \|M(k)\|_{\mathbb C^{3}}^{2},$$
and consequently
$\|A_{b}(\cdot,t)\|_{\mathfrak h}^{2}=\eta_{0}^{2}t\int_{\mathbb R}
K_{t}(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_{b}(E)$;

(b) (normalisation) if $M\ne0$, then for every $t>0$ the denominator
$\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_{b}(E)$ is finite and strictly positive,
so
$$P_{t}(B):=\frac{\int_{B}K_{t}(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_{b}(E)} {\int_{\mathbb R}K_{t}(E-\Delta)\,d\nu_{b}(E)}$$
defines a Borel probability measure on $\mathbb R$ with
$P_{t}(\mathbb R\setminus(0,\Lambda])=0$;

(c) (concentration) if $\nu_{b}=J_{b}\lambda$ for some $J_{b}\in
L^{1}(\lambda)$ with $J_{b}=0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere on
$\mathbb R\setminus(0,\Lambda]$, if $J_{b}$ is continuous at some $\Delta$ with
$0<\Delta<\Lambda$ and $J_{b}(\Delta)>0$, and if $f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb C$ is
continuous and bounded, then
$$\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_{\mathbb R}f\,dP_{t}=f(\Delta);$$

(d) (positivity) if $\nu_{b}=J_{b}\lambda$ with $J_{b}\ge0$
$\lambda$-almost everywhere and $J_{b}>0$ $\lambda$-almost everywhere on a
Borel set $B\subseteq\mathbb R$ of positive Lebesgue measure, then
$P_{t}(B)>0$ for every $t>0$;

(e) (tail concentration) under the hypotheses of (c), for every $\delta>0$,
$\lim_{t\to\infty}P_{t}\bigl(\{E:|E-\Delta|\ge\delta\}\bigr)=0$.

No dynamics, transition probability, rate, decay or physical identification is
asserted; the lemma computes an explicit kernel, its normalised push-forward
law and that law's limit.
